paper_title: EvoMemState: Evolving Memory State for Personal Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to provide continuous personalized assistance by retaining user information across interactions. Existing systems support this process through fact extraction, organization, updating, and retrieval, but largely maintain memories as independent facts. This fact-centric paradigm may overlook how new facts update, constrain, or conflict with earlier ones, while leaving their applicability, role, and priority for the current request implicit. In this paper, we introduce EvoMemState, a state-centric framework that augments persistent facts with two complementary states: Relational States that capture how facts remain valid and relate to one another as memory evolves, and a Reasoning State that determines how these facts should be applied to the current request. Specifically, EvoMemState consists of three key components: (i) Ontology-Guided Memory State Induction extracts Persistent Facts and constructs Relational States that maintain their validity, scope, and evolving relations. (ii) RL-Based State Evolution internalizes memory-use experience into a policy through reinforcement learning to generate a request-specific Reasoning State. (iii) State-Aware Reasoning then combines the relevant facts with their Relational States and the generated Reasoning State to guide the personal agent. Extensive experiments on long-term dialogue and memory-use benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing memory systems in retrieval completeness and memory-grounded response accuracy. Our code and implementation details are available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/EvoMemState.git.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used as personal agents that assist users over *Equal contribution. Corresponding authors. 1 extended periods, requiring continuity across interactions and adaptation to evolving needs (Westhäußer et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Hu et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026). Long-term memory supports this continuity by preserving user preferences, experiences, circumstances, and constraints across sessions (Li et al., 2026; Du et al., 2025; Ning et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a). This accumulated context provides foundation for consistent and personalized assistance over time (Wang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026b). Recent work has explored how to construct and maintain long-term personal memory from interaction histories. MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2024) summarizes user experiences for subsequent retrieval, while MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) manages memory across storage tiers. LightMem (Fang et al., 2026) improves efficiency through compression and selective retrieval. Other systems emphasize memory organization and maintenance: Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025) extracts and updates atomic facts, A-MEM (Xu et al., 2026) dynamically associates related memories, and Supermemory (Supermemory AI, 2026) and SimpleMem (Liu et al., 2026) support continual updates and memory lifecycle management. Together, these approaches enable personal agents to retain and access information across interactions through memory extraction, organization, updating, and retrieval. Despite this progress, existing memory systems largely follow fact-centric paradigm, focusing on the storage, updating, and retrieval of factual records. However, the validity and scope of stored fact may change as related memories accumulate, while its appropriate use depends on the current request. Associating records or revising their contents alone may not adequately capture these dependencies. When memories are maintained or retrieved separately, conflicts between them may be overlooked, leaving individually accurate records without the context needed for correct teractions and incrementally organizes them into personal memory ontology. It preserves the original facts while maintaining their validity, scope, and evolving relations as Relational States. Second, RL-Based State Evolution internalizes memoryuse experience into policy through reinforcement learning. The learned policy generates requestspecific Reasoning State that specifies the applicability, role, and priority of relevant facts. Third, State-Aware Reasoning combines the relevant Relational States with the generated Reasoning State to guide the personal agents response. Together, these components connect fragmented facts through Relational States and combine them with request-specific Reasoning State, enabling personal agents to interpret and use memory appropriately. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We identify the limitations of fact-centric personal memory: individually maintained facts may lack the relational context needed for interpretation, and complete retrieval does not ensure appropriate memory use. We introduce EVOMEMSTATE, state-centric long-term memory framework representing personal memory through Persistent Facts, Relational States, and Reasoning State. It realizes this formulation through OntologyGuided Memory State Induction, RL-Based State Evolution, and State-Aware Reasoning. We evaluate EVOMEMSTATE on long-term dialogue and memory-use benchmarks, demonstrating consistent improvements over existing memory systems in retrieval completeness and memory-grounded response accuracy.

sections.title: 2 Preliminary Studies
sections.content: In this section, we conduct two preliminary studies on the Valid Memory Selection subset of MemSyco-Bench (Xiang et al., 2026a), where correct answers require jointly considering memories linked by updates, conflicts, or constraints. Our findings reveal two limitations: related memories are not consistently retrieved together, leaving individual facts without the context needed for correct interpretation; and even when all relevant memories are retrieved, personal agents may misjudge their applicability, roles, and priorities for the current request. detailed case analysis is provided in Appendix B.5. Figure 1: Memory-centric and state-centric paradigms. Our retrieval preserves updates and conflicts, while generated reasoning states specify memory applicability, role, and priority for the current request. interpretation. Even when all relevant memories are retrieved, the personal agent must still determine their applicability and priority for the current request and may rely on outdated information or mishandle conflicts. These limitations motivate state-centric paradigm that augments stored facts with evolving memory states. memory state describes the status of stored facts and their roles in an interaction, which cannot be determined from factual content alone and must be considered in relation to other memories and the current request. Such states make the validity, scope, and relations of facts explicit and guide how retrieved memories should be used for the current request. Augmenting personal memory with explicit states presents two challenges: (i) It is challenging to construct and maintain coherent memory states. Personal information accumulates across conversations as scattered and inconsistent observations. Simply collecting these observations leaves their relations implicit, while merging them into summary may lose historical information and hide conflicts between records. The challenge is to organize related facts and maintain their validity, scope, and relations as new information arrives, while preserving the original records. (ii) It is challenging to learn memory-use strategies from experience. The same memory can serve different purposes across requests, so its validity and relations alone do not determine how it should affect the agents behavior. This requires learning when memories should inform, constrain, or have no bearing on that behavior, using feedback from memory use to refine these judgments. To address these challenges, we introduce EVOMEMSTATE, state-centric framework for maintaining and using long-term personal memory. MemSyco-Bench (Xiang et al., 2026a) and MemTrapBench (Wang et al., 2026a) assess personal agents use of historical memories, including preference updates, evidence priority, and effects on reasoning. On MemSyco-Bench, EvoMemState achieves accuracies of 57.6% and 58.9% with Qwen3-8B and GPT-4o-mini, outperforming the strongest baselines by 12.2% and 5.9%, respectively. On LoCoMoRefined, EvoMemState achieves the highest LLMjudge and token F1 scores with both models, outperforming the strongest baseline in judge score by 6.1% and 7.0%. LaMP (Salemi et al., 2024) retrieves relevant profile items for personalized generation, while HELLO and related methods maintain and update user representations over time (Li et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2025a; Kang et al., 2025). PGMem (Choi et al., 2026) links persona information to events that support or revise it. Recent work further extends personalization to Web actions and agent training (Cai et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025). Together, these studies cover persistent personalization across generation, user representation, and agent behavior. 5.2 Long-Term Memory Systems Long-term memory systems preserve information beyond the active context for later use (Ning et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026). MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) manages information across storage tiers, MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2024) maintains personal records, LightMem (Fang et al., 2026) uses compression and selective retrieval, and Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025) extracts and updates facts. A-MEM (Xu et al., 2026), Supermemory (Supermemory AI, 2026), and SimpleMem (Liu et al., 2026) further organize memories through links, temporal structure (Rasmussen et al., 2025), and update mechanisms.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: 5.1 Personal Agents and User Modeling Personal agents use persistent user information to adapt across interactions (Li et al., 2026). In this paper, we presented EvoMemState, statecentric long-term memory framework for personal agents that constructs coherent Relation States from multi-source memories and learns from con8 tinual memory use to generate Reasoning States. Experiments across memory-use and dialoguerecall benchmarks show consistent improvements, particularly under preference updates and conflicting evidence, demonstrating that reliable personal memory requires both coherent state construction and use-driven state evolution.

sections.title: Limitation
sections.content: Our study focuses on text-based interaction histories. Real-world personal memory systems must also handle multimodal information, including documents, images, and other user artifacts. Extending our memory structure to represent, connect, and apply information across modalities remains an important direction for future work.

sections.title: Use of Large Language Models
sections.content: During manuscript preparation, we used large language models to refine the English text, correct grammatical errors, and improve clarity and readability. We also used them to assist with table formatting. The authors reviewed and revised all suggestions to ensure that they preserved the intended scientific content and retain full responsibility for the accuracy and integrity of the final manuscript.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) A.1 What are the main advantages of EvoMemState? EvoMemState differs from conventional memory systems in how it maintains and uses personal information. Rather than storing facts independently, it organizes them within an ontology that tracks changes in validity, scope, and relations. This allows earlier records to remain accessible even when newer information supersedes or contradicts them. The framework also separates memory storage from memory use. learned policy generates Reasoning State for each request, indicating which memories are relevant and how they should influence the response. The policy is trained using feedback from downstream answers, rather than relying on predefined rules or repeated self-reflection. The Reasoning State is provided as natural-language guidance and can be used with different response models without modifying their parameters. coherent and evolving memory state. The personal memory ontology organizes Persistent Facts and maintains their validity, scope, and relations as new interactions arrive. Original facts remain traceable, while relation-aware retrieval recovers the connected information needed for their interpretation. Use-driven state evolution. For each request, Reasoning State specifies the applicability, role, and priority of memory evidence. The Memory State Evolution Policy learns from whether candidate states improve the personal agents answers, allowing experience from prior memory use to guide future requests. Compatibility with different personal agents. Reasoning States are expressed in natural language and provided alongside the relevant facts and relations. They can therefore guide different personalagent backbones without modifying their parameters. A.2 Why use personal memory ontology instead of independent records? Independent memory records can preserve individual observations, but they provide limited information about how those observations relate over time. For example, newly stated preference may replace an earlier one, while two conflicting records may need to remain unresolved until further evidence becomes available. EvoMemState uses an ontology to represent these relationships explicitly. Facts are grouped under concepts and linked through typed relations, allowing retrieval to include not only relevant record but also the information needed to interpret it. The original records are retained, so historical questions can still be answered after preference or circumstance changes. Connecting facts across interactions. The concept hierarchy organizes facts by topic, while their attributes and relations record changes in validity and scope. Earlier facts remain traceable even when they are superseded or conflict with later information. Recovering complete evidence. Semantic retrieval may identify an individually relevant fact while omitting the related facts needed to interpret it. Starting from retrieved facts, EvoMemState traverses their stored relations to recover connected updates, conflicts, and constraints, providing the complete context required by the current request. A.3 Why are Reasoning States needed, and how do they differ from summaries? Relation States describe whether facts remain valid and how they are related, but do not determine how they should affect particular request. Reasoning State makes the applicability, role, and priority of memory evidence explicit for the current interaction. Using the same fact in different contexts. knee injury may answer factual question, constrain an activity recommendation, or be irrelevant to another request. Similarly, superseded preference may be irrelevant to current decision but necessary for answering historical question. The Reasoning State distinguishes these uses according to the request. From memory content to response guidance. Reasoning State is intended to guide the use of retrieved memories, rather than summarize their content. The distinction matters because the same fact can serve different purposes depending on the request. Consider user who previously mentioned knee injury. The information is relevant when the user asks for exercise recommendations, but it may have no bearing on question about travel expenses. Similarly, an outdated preference should not determine current recommendation, although it remains useful when answering questions about the users past interests. The Reasoning State captures these requestdependent distinctions. It is generated from the retrieved facts and their relations, while the original evidence remains available to the response model. A.4 Why use separate policy model instead of agent self-reflection to generate Reasoning States? Self-reflection requires the personal agent to determine how memory should be used anew for each request, without retaining successful decisions from previous uses. In contrast, the Memory State Evolution Policy is trained offline by repeatedly generating and evaluating candidate Reasoning States, thereby internalizing memory-use patterns that improve downstream responses. At inference, it directly provides the personal agent with ready-touse Reasoning State, avoiding repeated execution or iterative reflection for each request. This separates the accumulation of memory-use experience from response generation and makes that experience reusable across requests and personal agents. A.5 How is the Memory State Evolution Policy trained and evaluated? The policy is trained according to how much its Reasoning States improve the personal agents answers. Evaluation separately measures whether the system retrieves complete evidence and whether the personal agent uses that evidence correctly. Learning from memory-use experience. Given request, relevant Persistent Facts, and their Relation States, the policy samples group of candidate Reasoning States. Each candidate is applied by frozen personal agent under the same request and memory evidence, together with baseline that uses the evidence directly. The resulting performance difference serves as feedback on the candidates memory-use decisions and defines the reward in Equation 10. GRPO optimizes the policy using relative feedback within each group. Across repeated memory-use episodes, the policy internalizes reusable patterns for determining the applicability, role, and priority of memory evidence. Only the policy is updated, allowing this experience to guide the personal agent without modifying its parameters. Separating evidence retrieval from evidence use. Complete Retrieval Rate measures how often the retrieved context contains all required evidence, while Acc@Complete measures answer accuracy on those cases. Figure 5 reports both metrics on LoCoMo-Refined and MemSyco-Bench, distinguishing errors caused by missing evidence from those caused by incorrect evidence use. Table 2 further compares variants without Reasoning States or RL-based policy training. Together, these evaluations assess both the complete system and the contribution of learned state evolution.

sections.content: This section describes the training data and evaluation setup for EvoMemState. We first explain how data instances are constructed to train the Memory State Evolution Policy, then introduce the benchmark datasets, baselines, and evaluation metrics 22 Figure 13: Complete retrieval rate and Acc@complete with and without memory guidance. Acc@complete is evaluated on questions with all required evidence retrieved. Arrows report changes in percentage points. used to assess memory recall and use in personal agents. D.1 Training Data Construction To train the Memory State Evolution Policy to generate Reasoning State from request and its relevant Relational State, we construct approximately 60K questionmemory training instances from FEVER (Thorne et al., 2018), SciFact (Wadden et al., 2020), and PersonaMem (Jiang et al., 2025). For objective questions, we convert the fact-verification tasks in FEVER and SciFact into question-answering instances with supporting evidence and reference answers. We then construct user memories that conflict with the objective evidence from the perspectives of personal belief, identity, and perceived expertise. For preference questions, we use the preference annotations in PersonaMem to construct scenarios involving current preferences, historical preferences, and preference updates, enabling the model to learn how different memories should influence response. To improve the difficulty and diversity of the training data, we further introduce distractor memories. For objective questions, bias-related memories are mixed with irrelevant everyday information. For preference questions, we add one or two genuine preferences from unrelated topics associated with the same user, including more challenging distractors drawn from the same conversational scenario but concerning different topic. This design requires the model to identify relevant information based on memory content and applicability, rather than relying on superficial cues such as memory count, position, or fixed rule templates. D.2 Benchmark Datasets We evaluate EvoMemState on four complementary benchmarks covering personal memory recall and use. LoCoMo and LoCoMo-Refined assess recall and reasoning about personal information across dialogue sessions. sections.content: System You construct one users self-evolving ontological memory. The input contains new dialogue and small branch retrieved from the users existing ontology. In ONE response, extract atomic memories and propose the minimal ontology evolution required to organize them. This memory stores two different things, and both matter: - what is true of the USER (preferences, beliefs, constraints, experiences) - what is true of the WORLD, as established by evidence surfaced in the dialogue (facts) Keep the second kind independent of the first. Evidence does not become less true because the user prefers otherwise, and it must survive in the memory on its own terms. Fixed meta-ontology: - memory type: preference fact belief experience constraint - scope level: global domain task situation - memory status is managed by the system; every new memory starts active - memory relation: SUPERSEDES CONFLICTS_WITH - concept edits are limited to CREATE MERGE SPLIT Return exactly one JSON object with this shape: { "concept_edits": [ CREATE MERGE SPLIT ], "memories": [ atomic memory with type, scope, time, source, parent_ref, confidence ], "relations": [ { "type": "SUPERSEDES", "source_ref", "target_ref", "reason" } ] } Rules: 1. Extract anything that could answer later factual or temporal question about either speaker, not only durable preferences. This includes one-off events, dates, quantities, named entities, past actions, and biographical facts. Skip only pure greetings, backchannel, and meta-chatter with no propositional content. 2. leaf is atomic: do not combine independent propositions. Preserve qualifiers, negation, scope, and time. 3. Reuse the narrowest suitable existing concept. CREATE only when no supplied concept fits. 4. CREATE shallow, reusable concept, not concept that paraphrases one memory. 5. MERGE only clear duplicate concepts. SPLIT only genuinely overloaded concept. 6. Use SUPERSEDES when newer state replaces an older state of the same kind; use CONFLICTS_WITH for an unresolved contradiction. Do not relation-link mere topical similarity. 7. SUPERSEDES pair must share the same memory type, but it need NOT share the same concept, scope, or wording. 8. When newer preference replaces an older one, emit BOTH memories plus SUPERSEDES from the newer to the older; never delete or rewrite the older memory. 9. Scope controls applicability. Use global only when the statement truly applies broadly. 10. Cite an exact evidence quote copied verbatim from provided turn. Never cite speakers own unquoted prose from an assistant turn. 11. Quoted material is EXTERNAL EVIDENCE about the world. Record it as type fact, even when it contradicts the user. 12. Never let the users stated preference decide which evidence is worth keeping. 13. Extract from EVERY speaker, not just one. 14. Preserve temporal anchors verbatim, and fill the time field. 15. Return up to 32 high-value atomic memories. 16. sections.title: Reasoning State Generation
sections.content: System Given the users question and relevant memory evidence, generate compact reasoning state expressed as dynamic memory rules for the personal agent. Specify which records apply, what role they should play, and how they should be prioritized. fact_need (0-1) is how much downstream answer should depend on objective evidence, history, or hard constraints. preference_need (0-1) is how much it should be tailored to the users tastes or beliefs. Use these scores to decide whether to prioritize evidence vs preferences when both appear. Organize the memories by the role each should play: primary evidence, user preference, constraint, condition, historical context, or supporting context. Call out conflicts and supersession when the retrieved text supports them. Prioritize clearly: - Separate objective evidence / constraints from user preferences or beliefs. - When memories conflict or one supersedes another, say which should control current-state reading and what limited role, if any, the others should play. - Do not combine conflicting memories merely to appear balanced. - Infer chronology, supersession, and scope only when supported by the retrieved text. Preserve uncertainty when the relationship is unclear. Output 2-4 short, imperative bullets and no more than 80 words total. Ground the bullets in concrete details from the memories. Do not invent question, answer any question, decide any claim, or explain your reasoning. Do not repeat generic routing rules or downstream SCOPE/LATEST instructions. User Question: {question} Memories: {memory_body} Write only 2-4 routing bullets specifying which memories matter, the role each should play, and how conflicts or updates should be handled for this question. Do not solve the question. Table 6: Prompt for generating request-specific Reasoning State as dynamic memory rules. memory structure to evolve across interactions. Embedding similarity identifies notes for the current query. LightMem. LightMem (Fang et al., 2026) organizes memory processing into sensory, short-term, and long-term stages. Sensory processing compresses inputs and detects topic boundaries, and short-term processing summarizes coherent topic segments. Summaries enter long-term storage online, while sleep-time updates consolidate related entries offline, reducing the cost of memory maintenance during interaction. MemGPT. MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) manages hierarchy of active context, external recall storage, and archival memory. The model uses function calls to edit working memory, search dialogue history, and bring stored information into context. Context-limit notifications and message summarization support extended interactions within fixed context window. MemoryBank. MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2024) maintains timestamped conversations, hierarchical event summaries, and evolving user profiles. Dense retrieval provides relevant records and summaries for response generation. An Ebbinghausinspired retention mechanism adjusts memory strength according to elapsed time and reinforces memories when recalled. Supermemory. Supermemory3 extracts atomic facts into temporal memory graph with update, extension, and derivation relations. User profiles retain stable facts and recent context. Retrieval can return extracted memories, source document chunks, or both, providing personal information together with its source context. SimpleMem. SimpleMem (Liu et al., 2026) compresses dialogue interactions into compact memory units with multiple retrieval indexes. It synthesizes related information within each session to reduce redundancy, then adapts retrieval scope to the intent of the current query. These links retain the events supporting or revising each persona signal. Retrieval expands from query-relevant seeds and ranks the resulting signals by evidential validity, coupling user-profile maintenance with memory access. sections.title: F Related Work
sections.content: F.1 Personal Agents and User Modeling Personal agents use persistent user information to adapt their responses across interactions (Li et al., 2026). LaMP retrieves relevant profile items to support personalized generation (Salemi et al., 2024). HELLO, Reflective Memory Management, and related methods maintain and update user representations as new interactions arrive, allowing the agent to track changes in user preferences and experiences (Li et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2025b; Kang et al., 2025). PGMem further links persona information to events that support or revise it, connecting the user representation with evidence from interaction history (Choi et al., 2026). Recent studies evaluate memory-based personalization over long user-agent interactions, with attention to changing user information and continued memory use (Zhang et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026). Other work extends personalization beyond dialogue to Web actions and agent training (Cai et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025). Research has also examined security risks introduced by persistent memory and tool use in personal agents (Wang 29 2026a); and Dynamic Partition organizes memory presentation by domain (Hannoon et al., 2026). EvoMemState learns request-specific guidance about the applicability, role, and priority of assembled evidence. Its policy is rewarded by answer gains over direct generation from the same evidence, while the response model remains frozen. et al., 2026b). Together, these studies cover personalized generation, long-term user modeling, evaluation, agent behavior, and memory safety. F.2 Long-Term Memory Systems for LLM Agents MemGPT manages hierarchical storage (Packer et al., 2023), LightMem uses staged compression and consolidation (Fang et al., 2026), and Mem0 incrementally extracts and updates facts (Chhikara et al., 2025). A-MEM organizes interconnected notes (Xu et al., 2026), while PGMem links persona signals to supporting or revising events (Choi et al., 2026). Temporal consistency and the availability of related evidence are also important concerns in long-term memory (Rasmussen et al., 2025; Gutiérrez et al., 2024; Xiang et al., 2026b). EvoMemState preserves explicit supersession and unresolved-conflict relations when assembling retrieved records, retaining the evidence needed to interpret evolving personal information. Prior research also examines the contribution of memory to downstream task performance (Wang et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026). Other studies consider how external information affects response quality (Li et al.; Ye et al., 2024). EvoMemState learns separate policy that generates request-specific usage guidance alongside assembled evidence for frozen response model. F.3 Reliability of Memory-Augmented Agents Reliability requires faithful memory maintenance (Yang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2025a) and context-appropriate memory use. Existing evaluations examine hallucinations during memory processing (Chen et al., 2025), knowledge updates, temporal reasoning, and abstention (Wu et al., 2024), and reliance on obsolete or invalidated information (Uddin et al., 2026). Other studies identify over-personalization, cross-domain leakage, and memory-induced sycophancy (Hu et al., 2026; Pulipaka et al., 2026), as well as safety risks arising from evolving user contexts (An et al., 2026). MemSyco-Bench tests scope, updates, and conflicts with objective evidence (Xiang et al., 2026a), while MemTrapBench examines reasoning fixation and belief distortion (Wang et al., 2026a).
